title: Pair Sum in a Search Tree
statement:
You get the root of a binary search tree with distinct values, and a number k. Return true if two different nodes have values that add up to k, and false otherwise.

The tree is given in level order with null for missing children.

examples.why: 8 + 8 would use the same node twice. No two different values reach 16.
A single node cannot pair with itself.

hints: Forget the tree for a moment: how do you find two numbers in an array that add to k?
Walk every node and remember the values you have seen in a set. Before adding a value, check whether k minus it is already there.
Or use the BST order: an inorder walk gives the values sorted, and two pointers from both ends find the pair.

explain.intuition:
This is the classic "two numbers adding to k" problem with the numbers stored in a tree instead of an array. The tree is just a container: visit every node, and for each value ask "have I already seen k − value?" A hash set answers that in O(1).

The search-tree property gives a second route. An inorder walk visits values in sorted order, and on a sorted list two pointers from both ends find a pair in one pass: if the sum is too small move the left pointer up, if too big move the right pointer down.
steps: Create an empty set seen and a stack (or recursion) to walk the tree.
For each node value v: if k − v is in seen, return true.
Otherwise add v to seen and continue with the children.
If the walk ends without a hit, return false.
pitfalls: Adding v to the set before checking k − v. Then k = 2v matches the node with itself (example 2).
Searching only one subtree for the partner. The partner can be anywhere, including above the current node.

solutions.title: Walk the tree with a seen-set
solutions.idea: Visit every node once; the pair exists as soon as k − value has been seen before.

solutions.title: Inorder to a sorted list, then two pointers
solutions.idea: The inorder walk of a BST is sorted. Squeeze two pointers from both ends of that list.

followups: Do it in O(h) extra space with two iterators: one walking the tree in order, one in reverse order.
Count all pairs that add to k instead of stopping at the first.
